name: Licochalcone A
lead: Licochalcone A is a chalcone-type phenol isolated from the roots of licorice species (Glycyrrhiza inflata and G. glabra).[1][2] In skincare it appears in moisturizers, sunscreens and post-treatment creams made for sensitive, red, irritated or acne-prone skin, and it is also discussed for a possible effect on pigment production.[4][11][12]

People use it to calm visible redness and irritation, to support acne routines, and to help skin look more even after procedures. Randomized trials of cosmetic formulations containing licochalcone A reported less redness in post-shaving irritation and UV-induced erythema models, and trials of multi-ingredient creams in acne have been run in several Asian and European settings.[7][8][9][10][12][13]

Laboratory research has reported antioxidant, antibacterial, antimalarial and anticancer activity,[1][5][6][7] and licorice flavonoids have been examined for tyrosinase inhibition.[4] Most human acne data come from products that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so its contribution alone cannot be separated.[8][9]
infobox: Soothing / anti-redness; examined for anti-melanogenic activity [4][12]
Ingredient in OTC moisturizers, sunscreens and post-procedure creams [11][12]

paras: Licochalcone A is found in cosmetic products for sensitive and acne-prone skin. A 2016 study paired it with 4-t-butylcyclohexanol, a compound that reduces TRPV1 activation, in a concept for sensitive skin and reported relief from stinging and a reduction of shaving-induced redness with a cream combining the two.[13]

Combination moisturizers containing licochalcone A, L-carnitine and decanediol have been used alongside adapalene gel, with intense pulsed light treatment, and as maintenance after acne treatment.[8][9][10][14] A sunscreen with an anti-inflammatory agent has been tested for pigmentation after picosecond laser treatment.[11]

In the 2006 study, licochalcone A reduced redness in a post-shaving model and in UV-induced erythema, and in cell experiments inhibited the oxidative burst of granulocytes, the release of PGE2 and LTB4, and the secretion of IL-6 and TNF-alpha.[12] The 2016 sensitive-skin work reported that licochalcone A reduced NF-kB signalling and PGE2 secretion in vitro.[13]

Six licorice flavonoids including licochalcone A were characterised in a 2013 study for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity.[2] A 1998 study reported superoxide-scavenging and antioxidative activity of retrochalcones from G. inflata,[3] and a 2005 study isolated licorice flavonoids and tested their inhibitory effect on tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin.[4]

Licochalcone A has been reported to inhibit growth of Plasmodium falciparum in vitro and to protect mice from P. yoelii infection,[5] to disrupt bacterial growth,[7] to inhibit Helicobacter pylori growth in vitro,[15] and to arrest PC-3 prostate cancer cells in the cell cycle.[6] A 2019 review collects in vitro and in vivo work on licochalcones,[16] and a 2022 review of natural products that target cancer glycolysis includes licochalcone A.[17] Neuroinflammation and NMDA neurotoxicity have been examined in cell and mouse models.[18][19]

Licochalcone A has the formula C21H22O4 and is isolated from the roots of Glycyrrhiza glabra or G. inflata.[1] Chalcones are precursors of flavonoids; licochalcones A through G have been described from licorice root.[16] Licorice root has a long history in traditional Chinese medicine.[16] Wikipedia lists generic hazard labelling for the pure chemical, which is relevant to handling the raw compound rather than finished cosmetic products.[1]

In the randomized trials of cosmetic creams that included licochalcone A, tolerability was a measured outcome: in the 2020 relapse-prevention trial, dryness, stinging or burning and itching did not differ between the active and vehicle sides,[9] and in the 2016 adapalene trial the moisturizer group had less irritation by corneometer and water-loss measurements.[14]
The 2006 randomized, vehicle-controlled trials found that licochalcone A significantly reduced erythema in a post-shaving irritation model and in UV-induced erythema.[12]

In acne, a double-blinded 8-week trial in 120 patients with mild to moderate acne compared adapalene alone, adapalene with an active moisturizer containing licochalcone A, L-carnitine and decanediol, and adapalene with placebo; the moisturizer group had significant reductions in inflammatory and total lesions without flare-ups, with less irritation, and the authors concluded it reduced adapalene side effects without reducing efficacy.[14][8] In a 2020 vehicle-controlled maintenance trial, 50 responders from an initial 110 patients used a moisturizer with licochalcone A, decanediol, L-carnitine and salicylic acid on one side of the face for 12 weeks and had significantly lower lesion counts than on the vehicle side.[9][10]

A 2020 split-face trial in 29 volunteers found that intense pulsed light photodynamic therapy plus an active cream with licochalcone A, L-carnitine and decanediol cleared lesions faster than light therapy alone and showed a lower melanin index at one time point, with the authors reporting improved post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[20] A 2022 split-face trial of a sunscreen with an anti-inflammatory agent in 59 patients after picosecond laser showed a trend toward less brown pigmentation that was not statistically significant.[11]
These are all multi-ingredient products except for the 2006 irritation work. No studies found on licochalcone A alone for pigmentation.

card.summary: A licorice-root chalcone used in soothing skincare, with lab hints of tyrosinase inhibition and only combination-product acne trials in humans.
card.note: Human data are multi-ingredient acne products; pigment and redness claims rest on lab work.

quick.overview:
Licochalcone A is a compound from licorice root that shows up in sensitive-skin and acne-care products. It is also discussed for possible brightening effects.
Human studies found were acne trials of moisturizers containing several actives, so its own effect cannot be isolated.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work reports antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and licorice flavonoids have been tested for tyrosinase inhibition.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists generic hazard labeling for the pure chemical, relevant to handling rather than finished products.

chain: Topical licochalcone A reduces inflammatory signalling in lab and skin-irritation models
Less visible redness and irritation, better tolerance of acne actives and procedures
angle.text: Licochalcone A is used in leave-on products to calm reddened or irritated skin, which makes the complexion look more even and helps people keep up with acne treatments such as adapalene. Its possible effect on pigmentation has so far been examined mainly in the lab and in combination products.
